[[Category:Glasgow Name Study]]

== Biography ==
James was the son of [[Glasgow-634|James Glasgow]] and [[Sheppard-2142|Phereby Sheppard]]. 
== Research Notes ==
=== Current Maryland and Smith County review, 23 October 2026 ===

'''Existing father 65% → 94% confident.''' The inspected closing family paragraph of Holloman’s biography lists a son James born about 1776 and identifies a son James as an executor in 1819. Those specific family roles match the existing James-2492, whose original biography defines him as the secretary’s son and associates him with the later Smith County household. His approximate North Carolina birth, the described family’s removal to Tennessee and his retained Smith County records form a coherent adult sequence. This supplies the explicit child passage missing from the earlier 65% review, rather than treating a head-only census as proof of parentage.

94% assesses this existing father–child profile pair, including the assignment of the named son to the Smith County adult. The article is one late secondary account; its son list and executor statement are not independent witnesses. The Smith County adult continuity is inferred, and a mistaken same-name assignment remains possible. The article cites Davidson County Wills and Inventories volume 7, 1816–1821, but the original 1819 will has not been read. Existing dates, mother and all other relatives are retained.

[https://www.ncpedia.org/biography/glasgow-james Charles R. Holloman, “Glasgow, James,” Dictionary of North Carolina Biography (1986), NCpedia revision December 2022] was read on 23 October 2026. This is a newly inspected passage in an existing citation, not a new source discovery. The original will was not inspected.

'''New possible son Wesley-2476, 35%.''' Select James Glasgow-2492, the older Smith County householder, as Wesley Guynn Glasgow-2476’s possible working father. Their maintained accounts cite James in Smith County in 1820 and 1840 and the younger Wesley/Neely household there in 1850. James’s approximate 1776 birth makes him about 42 at Wesley’s estimated 1818 birth, a comfortable direct generation. The older James is a specific existing local household, not an invented parent. This is the leading bounded catalogue comparison for the disconnected Wesley family; its same-county chronology is more specific than an otherwise unplaced Tennessee or Scottish Glasgow.

35% is a subjective, low-confidence estimate for the complete father-profile hypothesis. No inspected record calls Wesley James’s son, places them in one household, transfers land between them, or names Wesley’s parents. The cited 1820/1840/1850 census images and age-band counts were not newly inspected; FamilySearch required a security challenge and the linked Ancestry record required membership. Wesley’s memorial has no parent links, dates or photograph beyond an approximate birth/death note; it is not independent parent proof. Wesley’s identification with the indexed Neely and James’s earlier North Carolina ancestry are separate propositions. An uncle or other collateral relationship, another local James, an unrepresented father, and William-2130 (broad Tennessee context without a held Smith County association) remain alternatives. No mother is selected and no relative is moved solely because of a name, naming custom or Y-DNA premise.

=== Earlier assessments retained as history ===
=== Individual father review, 22 October 2026 ===

This dated review supersedes any earlier grade of this pair within the stated record scope. The existing father [[Glasgow-634]] is assessed at 65% (probable). James’s circa-1776 North Carolina birth and later Smith County records fit a son of the secretary who died in Tennessee. The NCpedia father citation is relevant, but its child passage is not held; head-only censuses do not identify a father.

Named child to the specific adult family role represented by the selected father; independent earlier ancestry is outside this assessment.

Next useful test: Read the child passage in the cited biography/family account and seek James’s Tennessee probate or contemporary family record.
